title: Reading a Recipe
bigQuestion: How do you turn a recipe card into food that comes out right?

story.title: Trail Mix for Twenty-Four
story.kicker: The recipe made enough for six. The field trip had twenty-four kids and one bus.
paragraphs: The fourth grade was going to the Field Museum on Friday. Mr. Okafor asked Dev's cooking group to make trail mix for the bus. Dev found a recipe in the class binder. At the top it said "Serves 6." There were twenty-four students on the list.

"Six goes into twenty-four four times," said Dev. "So we make it four times." Lena wrote the recipe on the board. 1 1/2 cups cereal. 1 cup pretzels. 1/2 cup raisins. 1/4 cup sunflower seeds. 2 tablespoons mini chocolate chips. Then she wrote a second column and started to multiply.

"Wait," said Marco. He had read the whole recipe first. "The last step says to keep it in a sealed bag so the pretzels stay crisp. And the note says no peanuts because of allergies. That is why it uses sunflower seeds." Dev nodded. He had almost grabbed the peanut jar.

They filled the big bowl. 6 cups cereal. 4 cups pretzels. 2 cups raisins. 1 cup seeds. 8 tablespoons of chips, which Lena counted out as 1/2 cup. Marco set a timer for two minutes and they stirred until it beeped. Then they bagged twenty-four scoops. Every bag was the same. Nobody went hungry on the bus.
story.think: What would have gone wrong if the group had not read the whole recipe first? How did they know to multiply by four?

lessons.title: Title, Yield and Time
lessons.mainIdea: The top of a recipe tells you what you are making, how much it makes and how long it takes.
reading: Hold a recipe card in your hand. The first line is the *title*. It tells you what you will make: Banana Muffins, Trail Mix, Cheese Quesadilla. Read it and picture the finished food. That picture helps you catch mistakes later.

Under the title is the *yield*. Yield means how much the recipe makes. It might say "Makes 12 muffins" or "Serves 4." Count the people you are feeding. If the yield is too small, you will need to make more. If it is too big, you will have leftovers.

Next comes the time. Some cards list prep time and cook time. Prep time is the washing, measuring and mixing. Cook time is the oven or the stove. Add them together. If the total is 45 minutes and dinner is at 6:00, you need to start by 5:15.

words.d: the name of the recipe, at the very top
how much a recipe makes, such as 12 muffins or 4 servings

look.title: The Top of the Card
look.text: Look at this card. Title: Banana Muffins. Makes 12. Prep time: 15 minutes. Bake time: 20 minutes. You have 14 people coming and it is 5:30. You want muffins on the table at 6:00.
look.prompt: Will one batch feed everyone? Is there enough time? What would you do?

check.q: What does the yield tell you?
check.why: Yield is the amount a recipe makes, like 12 muffins or 4 servings.

check.q: Prep time is 15 minutes and bake time is 30 minutes. How long in all?
check.why: Add prep and cook time together: 15 + 30 = 45 minutes.

check.q: A recipe serves 4. You are feeding 8. What do you know?
choices: You need to make it twice
check.why: 8 is two times 4, so you need two batches or a doubled recipe.

lessons.title: The Ingredient List
lessons.mainIdea: The ingredient list names each food and its exact amount, in the order you will use it.
reading: Below the time is the list of *ingredients*. An ingredient is one food that goes into the dish. Each line has two parts. First the amount, then the food: 1 cup rolled oats. 1/2 cup peanut butter. 2 tablespoons honey.

Read the whole line, not just the food. "1 cup chopped nuts" means measure a cup after chopping. "1 cup nuts, chopped" means measure first, then chop. "1/2 cup packed brown sugar" means press it down. The little words tell you how to measure.

Set every ingredient on the counter before you start. Check each one off the list. If you are missing one, you find out now, not with the batter half mixed. Missing a whole egg or the salt will change the dish.

words.d: one food that goes into a recipe
how much of an ingredient to use

look.title: Check the Counter
look.text: The list says: 1 cup oats, 1/2 cup sunflower butter, 1/3 cup honey, 1/2 cup mini chocolate chips, 1/4 teaspoon salt. On the counter are oats, sunflower butter, chocolate chips and the salt shaker. The mixing bowl is already out.
look.prompt: What is missing? When is the best time to find that out?

check.q: What two parts does each ingredient line have?
check.why: Each line gives how much and which food, like 1 cup oats.

check.q: "1 cup nuts, chopped" means what?
choices: Measure the nuts, then chop them
Chop the nuts and skip measuring
Use a cup of chopped and a cup of whole
check.why: When the word after the comma describes what to do, measure first, then do it.

check.q: Why set out every ingredient before mixing?
choices: It makes the food taste better
You find missing items before you start
Recipes say so on the card
check.why: Checking the list first means you never get stuck halfway with a missing food.

lessons.title: The Steps in Order
lessons.mainIdea: Follow the numbered steps in order, because each one sets up the next.
reading: The bottom of the card is the *steps*, also called directions. They are numbered. Step 1 might say "Heat the oven to 350 °F." Step 2 might say "Mix the dry ingredients in a large bowl." Do them in that order. Do not skip ahead.

Order matters because each step sets up the next one. If you add eggs before the butter is soft, the batter is lumpy. If you forget to heat the oven first, the batter sits and waits, and muffins come out flat. If you stir chocolate chips in before the flour, they sink.

Put your finger on the step you are doing. When it is done, move your finger down. Some cooks read each step out loud. This sounds slow. It is faster than starting over. A recipe is a set of steps in a row, and the row is the recipe.

words.d: the numbered directions that tell you what to do and in what order
to turn the oven on ahead of time so it is hot when the food goes in

look.title: Mixed-Up Muffins
look.text: Here are the steps out of order: fill the muffin cups; heat the oven to 375 °F; stir wet into dry until just mixed; bake 18 minutes; mix flour, sugar and baking powder in a big bowl; beat egg, milk and oil in a small bowl.
look.prompt: Put the six steps in the right order. Which step must be first, and why?

check.q: Why do you follow steps in order?
choices: Because it is a rule for tests
Because each step sets up the next
check.why: Each step gets something ready for the next one, so the order matters.

check.q: What goes wrong if you forget to preheat the oven?
choices: The batter waits and may bake flat
check.why: Batter that sits while the oven heats can lose its lift and bake flat.

check.q: What is a good way to keep your place in the steps?
choices: Keep a finger on the step you are doing
check.why: Marking your place with a finger keeps you from skipping or repeating a step.

lessons.title: Read It All First
lessons.mainIdea: Read the whole recipe from top to bottom before you touch a single ingredient.
reading: Before anything else, sit down and read the recipe *all the way through*. Top to bottom. Every line. This takes two minutes. It saves an hour. Surprises hide at the end. "Chill for 4 hours." "Let rise overnight." "Serve with the sauce from step 9."

While you read, ask three questions. Do I have every ingredient? Do I have every tool? Do I have enough time? A recipe that needs a blender is no good without a blender. A recipe that chills overnight is no good for tonight.

Look for warnings too. A note may say "nut-free" or "contains dairy." A step may say "ask an adult to drain the hot water." Reading first is how you find those. Then you start cooking with no surprises left.

words.d: from the first word to the last, with nothing skipped
an extra line on a recipe with a warning or a tip

look.title: The Surprise in Step 7
look.text: Look at Kai. It is 5:00 and dinner is at 6:00. He starts step 1 of a pasta bake without reading further. He mixes, layers and turns to step 7. It says: Bake 45 minutes, then rest 15 minutes before serving.
look.prompt: What time will dinner really be ready? What should Kai have done at 5:00?

check.q: What is the first thing to do with a new recipe?
choices: Read it all the way through
check.why: Reading first shows you every ingredient, tool and time before you begin.

check.q: Which surprise is most likely hiding at the end of a recipe?
choices: A long chilling or resting time
check.why: Late steps like chill 4 hours can change whether you have enough time.

check.q: A recipe needs a blender and you have none. When should you find that out?
choices: When the batter is half mixed
check.why: Reading the whole recipe first tells you which tools you need.

lessons.title: Short Words for Long Ones
lessons.mainIdea: Recipes use short abbreviations for units, and mixing up tsp and Tbsp changes the dish.
reading: Recipe cards are small, so words get shortened. A shortened word is an *abbreviation*. Learn these: tsp is teaspoon. Tbsp is tablespoon. c is cup. oz is ounce. lb is pound. qt is quart. pt is pint. min is minute and hr is hour.

The dangerous pair is tsp and Tbsp. A tablespoon holds three teaspoons. If the card says 1 tsp of salt and you read it as 1 Tbsp, you add three times the salt. The capital T is your clue. Big T means the big spoon. Small t means the small spoon.

Some cards use other symbols. °F is degrees Fahrenheit. A slash makes a fraction, so 1/2 is one half. Two numbers like 1 1/2 mean one and a half. When a word is new, stop and look it up. Guessing on a unit is the fastest way to ruin a dish.

words.d: a short way to write a longer word, like tsp for teaspoon
ounce; 8 fluid ounces make 1 cup, and 16 ounces make 1 pound

look.title: What the Short Words Mean
look.prompt: A card says 8 oz of cheese. A block at the store says 16 oz. How many blocks do you need?

check.q: What does Tbsp stand for?
check.why: Tbsp with a capital T is the tablespoon, the big spoon.

check.q: The card says 1 tsp salt. You read it as 1 Tbsp. What happens?
choices: The dish has too little salt
The dish has three times the salt
check.why: A tablespoon is 3 teaspoons, so the dish gets triple the salt.

check.q: What does 1 1/2 c mean?
choices: One cup and one more half of a teaspoon
check.why: 1 1/2 is one and a half, and c means cup.

lessons.title: Set a Timer
lessons.mainIdea: Set a timer for every cooking time, and check the food when it rings instead of guessing.
reading: A recipe says "Bake 18 to 20 minutes." Do not watch the clock in your head. Set a *timer*. Use the oven timer, a kitchen timer or a phone. Set it for the shorter time, 18 minutes. Say the number out loud as you set it.

When it rings, check the food. Muffins are done when a toothpick pushed in the middle comes out clean. Cookies are done when the edges turn golden. If the food is not ready, set the timer again for 2 more minutes. Never walk away from a hot oven or stove without a timer running.

Timers keep you safe as well as on time. A pot that boils dry can burn. A cookie sheet forgotten in the oven can smoke. At home, an adult should be in the kitchen when the oven or stove is on. The timer is your helper, not your replacement.

words.d: a tool that counts minutes and rings so you check the food
the signs that food is finished cooking, like golden edges or a clean toothpick

look.title: Times From One Recipe Card (example)
look.cite: example times from a class muffin recipe
look.prompt: How many minutes from start to finish? If the muffins must be ready at 6:00, when do you start?

check.q: The card says bake 18 to 20 minutes. What do you set the timer for?
check.why: Set the shorter time first, then check and add minutes if needed.

check.q: How can you tell muffins are done?
choices: A toothpick in the middle comes out clean
check.why: The timer tells you when to check; a clean toothpick shows the middle is baked.

check.q: Why should a timer always be running when the oven is on?
choices: So the oven does not lock
So food is not forgotten and burned
So the recipe card stays clean
check.why: A forgotten pan can burn or smoke; the timer reminds you to check.

lessons.title: Doubling a Recipe
lessons.mainIdea: To double a recipe, multiply every ingredient by 2 and write the new amounts before you start.
reading: A recipe serves 4 and you have 8 people. You need to *double* it. Doubling means times two. Write the recipe down again with a second column. Multiply each amount by 2. 1 cup becomes 2 cups. 1/2 cup becomes 1 cup. 3/4 cup becomes 1 1/2 cups.

Spoons work the same way. 1 tsp becomes 2 tsp. 1 1/2 tsp becomes 3 tsp, which is 1 Tbsp. 2 Tbsp becomes 4 Tbsp, which is 1/4 cup. Trade up to a bigger tool when you can. Four tablespoons is slower than one 1/4 cup.

Write every new amount down before you measure. Doing the math in your head while you pour is how mistakes happen. Baking time does not double. Two pans of muffins bake about as long as one. Use a bigger bowl, and check the food with a timer.

words.d: to make twice as much by multiplying each amount by 2
to add the same number over and over; 3 times 2 is 6

look.title: Two Columns
look.text: The card says: 2 cups flour, 3/4 cup sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1 egg, 1 cup milk. Draw a second column and double every line. Then pick the fastest tool for each new amount.
look.prompt: What is the doubled amount of baking powder, and which single spoon measures it?

check.q: You double 3/4 cup of sugar. How much do you need?
You double 1 1/2 tsp of vanilla. What is the fastest way to measure it?
check.why: 1 1/2 tsp times 2 is 3 tsp, and 3 tsp = 1 Tbsp.

check.q: What should you do before measuring a doubled recipe?
check.why: Writing the new amounts first keeps math mistakes out of the bowl.

lessons.title: Halving a Recipe
lessons.mainIdea: To halve a recipe, divide every ingredient by 2, and use spoon equivalents for the tricky ones.
reading: Sometimes you need less. A recipe makes 24 cookies and you want 12. You *halve* it. Halving means dividing by 2. 1 cup becomes 1/2 cup. 1/2 cup becomes 1/4 cup. 2 Tbsp becomes 1 Tbsp. 1 tsp becomes 1/2 tsp.

Some amounts get tricky. Half of 1 Tbsp is 1 1/2 tsp. Half of 1/4 cup is 2 Tbsp. Half of 1/3 cup is 2 Tbsp plus 2 tsp. Half of 1 egg is hard. Beat the egg in a small bowl and use about half of it. Write each new amount down before you begin.

Halving changes the pan, too. Half a batch of brownies in the full-size pan bakes thin and dry. Use a smaller pan or fewer muffin cups. The oven stays at the same temperature. Start checking a few minutes early, because a smaller amount can cook a little faster.

words.d: to make half as much by dividing each amount by 2
to split into equal parts; 6 divided by 2 is 3

look.title: Half a Batch of Brownies
look.text: The card says: 1 cup sugar, 1/2 cup butter, 2 eggs, 1/3 cup cocoa, 1/2 cup flour, 1/4 tsp salt. Makes 16 brownies in a 9-inch pan. You want 8 brownies. Write the halved amounts. The 1/2 cup butter is the tricky one.
look.prompt: What is the halved amount of each line? What pan would you use for 8 brownies?

check.q: You halve 1/2 cup of butter. How much do you use?
check.why: 1/2 divided by 2 is 1/4 cup, which is also 4 tablespoons.

check.q: Half of 1 Tbsp is how much?
check.why: 1 Tbsp is 3 tsp, and half of 3 tsp is 1 1/2 tsp.

check.q: What changes when you halve a pan of brownies?
choices: The oven temperature drops by half
check.why: Half the batter needs a smaller pan, or it bakes thin and dry.

lessons.title: Trail Mix, Times Four
lessons.mainIdea: To multiply a recipe by 4, multiply every line by 4 and trade up to the biggest tool that fits.
reading: Here is the class trail mix. Serves 6. 1 1/2 cups round oat cereal. 1 cup small pretzels. 1/2 cup raisins. 1/4 cup sunflower seeds. 2 Tbsp mini chocolate chips. You need 24 servings. 24 divided by 6 is 4. So you make the recipe *times four*.

Multiply each line by 4. Cereal: 1 1/2 times 4 is 6 cups. Pretzels: 4 cups. Raisins: 2 cups. Seeds: 1 cup. Chips: 2 Tbsp times 4 is 8 Tbsp, which is 1/2 cup. Write each new amount next to the old one. Check it twice.

Pour everything into the biggest bowl in the kitchen. Stir with a big spoon until the chips are spread out. Scoop about 1/2 cup into each of 24 bags. Seal every bag so the pretzels stay crisp. No stove, no knife, and everyone gets the same amount.

words.d: multiplied by 4, or made four times as much
the amount of food for one person

look.title: Trail Mix for 24 (example)
look.cite: example recipe from this chapter, multiplied by 4
look.prompt: Which line came from 2 tablespoons? How many cups of mix is that in all?

check.q: A recipe serves 6 and you need 24 servings. What do you multiply by?
check.why: 24 divided by 6 is 4, so every amount is multiplied by 4.

check.q: 1 1/2 cups of cereal times 4 is how much?
check.why: 1 1/2 times 4 is 6 cups.

check.q: 2 Tbsp of chips times 4 is 8 Tbsp. What is that in cups?
check.why: 16 Tbsp = 1 cup, so 8 Tbsp = 1/2 cup.

lessons.title: No-Bake Bites, Step by Step
lessons.mainIdea: A no-bake recipe still needs every step in order, real measuring and a timer for chilling.
reading: This recipe uses no oven and no stove. Oat Bites. Makes 12. 1 cup rolled oats. 1/2 cup sunflower butter or peanut butter. 1/3 cup honey. 1/2 cup mini chocolate chips. 1/4 tsp salt. Read it all first. Check for nut allergies. Wash your hands for 20 seconds.

Step 1: Spoon oats into the 1 cup dry cup and level it. Pour into a bowl. Step 2: Wipe a little oil in the 1/2 cup and measure the sunflower butter. Step 3: Measure the honey the same way in the 1/3 cup. Step 4: Add the chips and salt. Stir until no dry oats show.

Step 5: Cover the bowl and put it in the *refrigerator*. Set a timer for 30 minutes. Cold dough is easier to roll. Step 6: Roll into 12 balls about the size of a walnut. Keep them in a sealed container in the refrigerator. Honey is not for babies under one year, so keep these for bigger kids.

words.d: a recipe that needs no oven or stove
the cold box that keeps food at or below 40 °F
to cool food in the refrigerator until it is firm

look.title: Oat Bites That Fell Apart
look.text: Look at Rosa's tray. She measured everything, stirred it well and rolled the balls right away. They were sticky and fell apart in her hands. She skipped step 5 to save time. The chips also sank to the bottom of the bowl.
look.prompt: Which step did Rosa skip? How long should she have waited, and how would she know?

check.q: How long should the oat bite dough chill before rolling?
check.why: The recipe says chill 30 minutes so the dough is firm enough to roll.

check.q: How do you measure the sticky sunflower butter?
choices: Wipe a little oil in the cup first
Pack it like brown sugar and skip leveling
check.why: A thin coat of oil lets sticky food slide out so the whole amount goes in.

check.q: Why do you read the whole recipe before step 1?
choices: To find warnings, tools and the chilling time
check.why: Reading first shows the allergy note, the tools and the 30-minute chill.

review.q: Where on a recipe do you find how much it makes?
review.why: The yield, like Makes 12 or Serves 4, sits under the title.

review.q: What should you do before touching any ingredient?
review.why: Reading it all first finds missing tools, long chill times and warnings.

review.q: What does c stand for on a recipe card?
review.why: c is the abbreviation for cup.

review.q: Which abbreviation means the big spoon?
review.why: Tbsp with a capital T is the tablespoon.

review.q: A recipe says bake 12 to 14 minutes. What do you do?
choices: Set a timer for 12 minutes and check
Watch the clock in your head
review.why: Set the shorter time, check for doneness, then add minutes if needed.

review.q: You double 1/2 cup of raisins. How much do you need?
You halve 1/4 cup of seeds. How much do you use?
review.why: 1/4 cup is 4 Tbsp, and half of that is 2 Tbsp.

review.q: Why do the steps in a recipe come in a numbered order?
choices: So you can skip to the end
Because each step sets up the next one
review.why: Order matters; a step done too early or too late changes the dish.
